passage: The replacement of the scroll by the codex is one of the quiet revolutions in the history of reading. In the Mediterranean world of the early centuries of the common era, a book was usually a long roll of papyrus, wound on itself and read by unrolling one column at a time; within a few hundred years the dominant form had become the codex, a stack of folded sheets bound along one edge, which remains the shape of most books today. The customary explanation for the change is economy: a codex uses both sides of its writing material, it packs more text into less volume, and it is easier to carry. All of this is true, and none of it is quite enough.

The economic story struggles with timing. If thrift alone had driven the change, one would expect the codex to have spread fastest where writing material was scarce and to have triumphed as soon as its savings were obvious. Instead it lingered for generations as a humble format for notebooks, accounts and school exercises, while prestigious literature stayed on the roll. Its adoption was uneven in ways that cost does not explain; some communities, early Christian ones among them, seem to have taken it up well before their neighbours, for reasons that probably had as much to do with identity and use as with price.

A more illuminating difference lies in how the two forms allow a reader to move through a text. A scroll is constructed for continuous reading from beginning to end: to find a passage near the middle, one must wind through everything that precedes it, and comparing two distant passages is awkward enough that readers leaned heavily on memory instead. A codex, by contrast, can be opened anywhere. A finger can hold one place while the eye checks another; a page can be marked, numbered and returned to. The codex, in other words, made the text navigable, and navigation changed what reading could be. A legal compilation, a book of scripture to be cited in argument, a technical manual to be consulted rather than recited: these are works one enters at a point rather than travels through, and they suit the codex far better than the roll.

It would be a mistake to convert this into a narrative of inevitable progress. Readers of rolls were not deprived; they cultivated habits of memorisation and recitation that served their purposes admirably, and something of that intimacy with a whole text may have been lost when books became places in which to look things up. Nor did the codex create consultative reading out of nothing. But the form encouraged certain practices and discouraged others, and over centuries the encouragement told. The later apparatus of the book, page numbers, tables of contents and indexes, would have been nearly pointless on a roll. It is the codex's logic worked out in full.

passage: Among the stories collected in the Zhuangzi, one of the best known concerns an enormous tree. A master carpenter passes it without a second glance, and when his apprentice asks why so magnificent a specimen has been ignored, he explains that its wood is good for nothing: boats made from it would sink, coffins would rot and tools would split. That night the tree appears to the carpenter in a dream and rebukes him, pointing out that trees bearing fruit are stripped and broken and that trees with fine timber are cut down before their time; its own uselessness, it explains, is precisely the reason it has lived so long and grown so large.

The usual moral drawn from the story is a prudent one: in a dangerous world, conspicuous talent invites exploitation, and the wise keep their heads down. That reading has support in the text, which elsewhere praises figures who survive by escaping notice. But it makes the story smaller than it is. The carpenter's mistake is not merely that he underrates the tree; it is that he assumes the only question worth asking about a tree is what it is good for to a carpenter. The tree's reply amounts to the observation that usefulness is always usefulness to someone, for some purpose, and that a thing seen only through that lens is not really seen at all.

This point has lost none of its edge. We are surrounded by institutions that measure things by their contribution to some further end, and we have grown skilled at the carpenter's glance. A subject of study is asked to justify itself by the jobs it leads to, a stretch of land by the revenue it can produce, an hour of a person's time by what it yields. Each of these questions is reasonable on its own, and institutions that never asked them would be failing in their responsibilities. What the story warns against is letting one of them become the only question, so that whatever cannot answer it, a friendship, a landscape, an afternoon of unhurried conversation, is passed by as if it were not there.

It would be a mistake, though, to read the story as a rejection of usefulness as such. Boats and coffins must be made from something, and a world of nothing but magnificent useless trees would be a hard place to live. The story's target is narrower and more interesting: the habit of mind that cannot see a tree as anything other than timber not yet cut, and that mistakes the list of its own purposes for an inventory of what the world contains.

passage: Defenders of nudging, the practice of steering choices by altering how options are presented rather than by forbidding or taxing any of them, have a ready answer to the charge that it is manipulative. Someone, they point out, must decide which option on a form is pre-selected, which dish stands at eye level in a canteen and which paragraph of a letter comes first; since there is no presentation without some arrangement, the choice is not between influencing people and leaving them alone but between influencing them thoughtfully and influencing them carelessly. The argument is sound as far as it goes, and critics who speak as though an unarranged menu were available are attacking a position nobody holds.

Yet the argument from inevitability answers a weaker objection than the one that matters. What troubles the more careful critics is not that choice architects influence us, which is unavoidable, but that many of the most effective nudges work precisely to the extent that they go unnoticed. A default enrolment in a savings scheme succeeds partly because inertia keeps people where they were placed, but also because many never register that a decision was made on their behalf; a smaller plate reduces consumption chiefly when diners do not reflect that they have been served less. Influence of this sort does not engage the faculties by which people govern themselves, but routes around them.

One way to sharpen the worry is to ask whether a given nudge would survive disclosure. Suppose a canteen posted a notice explaining that fruit had been placed at the front because the management wanted employees to eat more of it. If the arrangement continues to work, its power did not depend on concealment, and it begins to look less like manipulation than like a reminder. If it stops working once explained, that is evidence that it relied on a gap between what people were doing and what they understood themselves to be doing, and an institution that relies on such gaps owes its public a justification that it cannot easily give in public.

The test is not decisive in every case, and it should not be mistaken for a general condemnation. Some nudges would plainly survive disclosure: a letter telling people that most of their neighbours pay their taxes on time would plausibly work whether or not recipients knew why it had been sent, since the information is itself the influence. Others might fail it for innocent reasons, because a disclosure can itself distract, or can provoke a reflexive contrariness that has nothing to do with the merits of the option. What the test accomplishes is to shift the debate from an unanswerable question, whether influence is present, to an answerable one, whether the influence could be avowed. That shift concedes to the defenders everything their best argument actually establishes, and withholds from them only what it never established.

options.B: conclusive proof that the institution using it has acted manipulatively and must abandon it.

options.D: a sign that disclosure is itself distracting and so should not be expected of institutions.

passage: For much of the twentieth century, anthropologists sorted the ties they recorded into two kinds. Some were 'real', resting on birth and descent; others were 'fictive', a convenient label for godparents, sworn brothers, adopted children and the many other relations that people treated as kinship but that did not, so the observer thought, rest on blood. The distinction seemed merely descriptive, and it took some time to see that it carried a theory with it: that the true foundation of kinship is biological, and that everything else is imitation.

The difficulty is that many of the people being described did not share the theory. In a number of societies, people become kin by eating food grown on the same land, by living in the same house, or by being nursed at the same breast. Under Islamic law, for instance, children nursed by the same woman are barred from marrying one another, much as siblings by birth would be; the tie created by milk is not a metaphor for kinship but a form of it. In such places, ties made in these ways may carry the same obligations of help, hospitality and mourning as ties of birth. Where relatedness is understood to accumulate through feeding and sharing over years, to call such ties fictive is not to describe them but to overrule the people who live them.

This is not an argument that biology is irrelevant. Birth is, almost everywhere, one of the most powerful ways of reckoning who belongs to whom, and an attempt to dissolve it entirely into choice would be its own kind of distortion. The point is narrower: biology is one idiom of relatedness among several, and which idioms count, and how much, varies from place to place. Nor is the West an exception that proves the biological rule. Adoption, the blended families formed by remarriage, and the arrangements made possible by donated eggs and sperm all require people to decide, often painfully, whether a tie of birth or a tie of care should prevail when the two come apart.

Seen this way, kinship is something people do as well as something they are born into. The older vocabulary was not useless, since it pointed to real differences in the ways ties are formed and maintained. Its error lay in treating one culture's answer to the question of what makes people kin as the standard against which every other answer was to be measured, and in mistaking that answer for a fact of nature rather than a choice that other peoples had made differently.

options.B: metaphorical, because it is modelled on the bond between brothers and sisters.
options.C: fictive, because it does not rest on birth or descent.
options.D: real, because it carries the same bar on marriage that a tie of birth carries.

passage: When a patient can no longer decide for herself, someone else must decide for her, and the question is on what basis. The answer favoured in much of modern medical ethics is that the surrogate, usually a close relative, should choose as the patient would have chosen had she been able to. This standard of substituted judgement has an obvious appeal. It extends the patient's autonomy beyond the point at which she can exercise it, so that even when she is unconscious, her values rather than anyone else's continue to govern what is done to her body. The older alternative, that the surrogate should simply choose whatever is in the patient's best interests, looks paternalistic by comparison, since it invites others to put their idea of a good outcome in place of hers.

The appeal is real, but it depends on there being something for the surrogate to reconstruct. Sometimes there is. A patient who said repeatedly, while healthy, that she would never want to be kept alive on a ventilator has left a clear instruction, and a daughter who honours it is doing exactly what the standard asks. Far more often, however, the situation that arises is one the patient never considered. She may have had firm views about dying at home but none about a trial of dialysis that offers a modest chance of recovery and a large chance of prolonged discomfort. To ask what she would have chosen here is to ask a counterfactual question to which there may be no fact of the matter. The surrogate who answers it confidently is not discovering the patient's will; he is extrapolating from scraps, and the extrapolation is shaped, inevitably, by his own hopes and fears.

This would matter less if the fiction were harmless, but it has two costs. The first is that it hides the surrogate's own judgement behind the patient's name, so that a decision which ought to be open to discussion, with doctors and with other relatives, is presented as beyond discussion: this is simply what she would have wanted. The second is subtler. Families often find substituted judgement consoling precisely because it seems to relieve them of responsibility, and that consolation is not to be despised. But a consolation bought by pretending is fragile, and relatives who later doubt that they read the patient correctly may suffer more than they would have if they had been told, from the start, that they were being asked to judge what was best for her.

The remedy is not to abandon substituted judgement but to confine it to cases where the patient's own wishes are actually known and actually bear on the decision, and to say plainly, in all other cases, that the surrogate is choosing on the patient's behalf what seems best for her. Honesty about which standard is in play is itself a form of respect for the patient.

passage: Spoken irony rarely needs announcing. A slight drag on a word, a flattened pitch, a pause before the punchline: listeners pick up such cues without noticing that they have done so, and the speaker relies on them without noticing either. Writing, however expressive in other respects, strips most of them away. For centuries this mattered less than it might have, because the written forms people used for personal exchange, letters above all, were slow, composed and long enough to establish their own tone over several paragraphs. A letter writer who wished to be ironic had room to prepare the reader for it.

The short typed message removes that room while keeping the pace of speech. Exchanges happen in seconds, between people who often know each other well enough to joke, in fragments too brief to carry their own context. The result is a familiar variety of communicative accident. A remark meant as affectionate teasing arrives as a rebuke; a dry agreement reads as sincere enthusiasm, or the reverse. The writer, who heard the intended tone in his own head as he typed, is often the last to see that it was not on the screen.

Writers have not, however, accepted this deprivation quietly. Over the past few decades they have built, without any committee to guide them, a supplementary system of signals: the small faces and symbols that can be appended to a sentence, the strategic use of capitals and repeated letters, even the presence or absence of a full stop, which among some groups of writers has come to make a short reply sound curt. It is common to lament these devices as a decline in the standards of written language. That complaint misses what they are for. They are not a lazy substitute for vocabulary but a written prosody, an attempt to restore precisely the cues that typing removed.

Yet the new system has a weakness that spoken prosody largely lacks. The meaning of a rising tone is shared across most speakers of a language; the meaning of a particular symbol or a missing full stop is settled within smaller circles and changes quickly. A face that one group uses to soften a criticism may strike another as mocking, and a message read across a gap of age or community can misfire precisely because the writer took care to mark its tone. The invention of written prosody, in other words, has not abolished misreading so much as relocated it, from the gap between voice and text to the gap between the conventions of different readers.

options.B: followed strict conventions that told every reader exactly when a writer intended to be ironic.

passage: For much of the last century it was an article of faith among progressive architects that ornament was a kind of lie. A building, they argued, should declare its structure and its purpose plainly; carving and moulding added cost without adding use, and they disguised what a building really was beneath a costume borrowed from some other age. The argument had moral force, and it produced buildings of great clarity. It also rested on a narrow idea of what counts as use.

Consider what ornament has traditionally done: a carved surround tells a stranger which of many openings is the entrance, so that nobody needs to read a sign to find the way in. A band of moulding at the level of the first floor breaks a tall wall into parts that a human eye can measure, so that a passer-by senses the height of the building in storeys rather than as an undifferentiated cliff. Projecting mouldings over windows throw rain clear of the glass and, as they weather, gather their stains in a pattern that reads as intended rather than as decay. Even purely figurative ornament, a row of leaves or a face above a door, offers the eye something to rest on at walking pace, which is the pace at which most people meet most buildings. These are uses, though not of the kind that appear in a structural calculation.

The critics were right about one thing: ornament applied without regard to any of these purposes, stuck on to a facade like a label on a jar, is as dishonest as they said, and much commercial building of their day was exactly that. But the remedy they chose, to strip surfaces bare, threw away the work along with the pretence. A blank wall is not neutral, for it tells the stranger nothing about where to go in, it offers no measure of scale, and it weathers into streaks that look like neglect because nothing in its design anticipated them. The plain building is honest about its structure and silent about almost everything else that a person on the street needs to know.

The more useful question, then, is not whether a building should be ornamented but what its ornament is for. Asked in that way, the question rules out a good deal of pastiche, the reproduction of historical detail for its associations alone. It also rules out a good deal of austerity that passes itself off as rigour, and it returns the judgement of a facade to the people who have to find their way past it.

passage: A familiar demonstration from the study of chess runs as follows. A position from a real game is shown for a few seconds and then removed, and players are asked to reconstruct it on an empty board. Strong players replace most of the pieces correctly, while novices manage only a handful, and the obvious conclusion is that strong players simply have better memories. The less obvious and more instructive part of the demonstration comes next. When the same pieces are scattered at random, in arrangements that could never arise in play, the masters' advantage largely disappears, and they do little better than beginners.

What the masters possess, then, is not a larger store for holding pieces but a different way of seeing them. Years of play have given them a vocabulary of familiar configurations, a castled king with its pawns in front, a bishop aimed down a long diagonal, and they take in a position as a few such units rather than as two dozen separate pieces. A novice looking at the same board sees wood on squares. The master sees a situation, and often, before any conscious calculation has begun, a sense of what the situation calls for.

Similar observations have been made in fields as different as radiology, birdwatching and the reading of geological maps, where experienced specialists frequently report knowing that something is wrong with an image within a second or two, before they can say what it is. The birdwatcher who names a distant species from the way it flies, long before any marking can be made out, is drawing on the same resource. It is tempting to describe this as intuition, as though it were a mysterious faculty standing apart from knowledge. It is better described as knowledge that has been absorbed into perception, so that it no longer needs to be consulted, because it shapes what is seen in the first place.

This view has practical consequences, though they are easily overstated. If expertise lies partly in the eye, it cannot be fully transmitted by rules and explanations; the learner has to look at a great many cases, with feedback, until the patterns become visible. But perception is not the whole of expertise. Masters still calculate, and careful specialists still check their first impressions, because a pattern that is recognised instantly can also be misrecognised instantly. The trained eye is fast and usually right within the territory that trained it, and that qualification matters: presented with a case unlike those it has learned from, its speed becomes a liability rather than an asset.

passage: In the large households of the nineteenth century, the best servant was the one who was least noticed. Grand houses were built with back staircases so that maids carrying coal or slops need never meet the family on the main stairs, and bells rang in a basement corridor so that a summons could be issued without anyone having to see who answered it. In some houses servants were expected to turn aside, even to face the wall, when a member of the family passed. It is tempting to read all this as snobbery, a taste for keeping inferiors out of sight, but snobbery explains less than it seems to. The invisibility of servants was not a by-product of the genteel household; it was one of the things the household was for.

What a gentleman's house displayed, above all, was ease: meals that appeared, fires that were lit, linen that was clean, all without visible effort. The ease was manufactured by a great deal of labour, and the labour had to be hidden for the ease to be believed. A servant glimpsed scrubbing a step was a reminder that comfort had a cost and a source; a servant unseen allowed the family to experience comfort as a natural condition of their kind of life. In this sense the architecture of concealment did not merely reflect a social hierarchy but helped to produce one, by allowing one class to appear exempt from necessity.

Large-scale domestic service of this kind has largely disappeared, and it is easy to assume that its logic went with it. Yet much of the modern service economy seems designed to recreate the same experience by other means. Food arrives at the door from a kitchen the customer never sees, carried by a courier who is a first name on a screen. Offices are cleaned at night, after the staff have gone home. Apps promise that groceries, laundry and repairs will simply happen, and their designers speak, revealingly, of removing friction, as though the friction in question were not, very often, the encounter with another person who is doing the work.

The comparison must not be pressed too far. The modern courier or cleaner is not bound to a single household, keeps hours that end, and has legal protections that a Victorian scullery maid lacked; to call such workers servants is to erase real gains. But the aspiration that the old houses expressed in brick and bells, the wish to receive service without meeting the server, has proved remarkably durable. What has changed is less the wish than the means of satisfying it, and the means are now available to far more people than ever owned a back staircase.

passage: The line-judgement experiments of the 1950s are among the most retold stories in psychology, and the moral usually drawn from them is a gloomy one. A participant sits among strangers who, one after another, give an obviously wrong answer about which of several lines matches a standard; when the participant's turn comes, he often repeats their error. The lesson, we are told, is that ordinary people will deny the evidence of their own eyes rather than stand apart from a crowd. This reading has become so familiar that it is easy to forget how much interpretation it smuggles in.

Begin with the numbers that the gloomy version tends to leave out. On the critical trials, most of the answers participants gave were correct, and a sizeable share of people never yielded at all. A study that is remembered as a demonstration of conformity could as easily be remembered as a demonstration of independence under strange and uncomfortable conditions. Which of these stories gets told says more about the teller than about the data.

More important is the question of what yielding meant. Outside the laboratory, when several people who seem competent and sincere all report the same thing, the rational response is to give their reports considerable weight, even against one's own impression. Our senses err, and other people are among the best instruments we have for catching their errors. A participant who reasoned, 'I cannot see why they are all saying this, but it is unlikely that every one of them is mistaken,' was not abandoning reason; he was applying a rule that serves well almost everywhere except in a room deliberately arranged to defeat it. On this view much of what looks like spineless deference is better described as informational influence: treating others as evidence.

None of this means that the pressure in the room was imaginary. Variations in which participants wrote their answers privately, rather than announcing them aloud, produced far less agreement with the majority, which suggests that some yielding was about avoiding embarrassment rather than about belief. Participants interviewed afterwards also described acute discomfort, and some admitted that they had answered against what they saw. Normative pressure, the wish to fit in, was real. The point is not that it was absent but that it was only part of the picture, and that collapsing everything into it produces a caricature.

The caricature matters because it shapes the remedies we prescribe. If people conform because they are weak, the cure is to exhort them to be brave. If they conform partly because they are sensibly using others as sources of information, the cure is better information: making dissent visible, so that a single honest voice breaks the appearance of unanimity, and designing institutions in which the reasons behind a majority view can be inspected rather than merely counted.

passage: Arguments about charity tend to divide into two camps. On one side are those who hold that money given to help others should go wherever it will do the most good, which, given the vast differences in what a sum can buy in different places, often means far from home. On the other are those who insist that we owe something special to our own: our town, our region, our country. The first camp accuses the second of parochialism dressed up as loyalty; the second accuses the first of a cold arithmetic that would dissolve every bond that makes moral life recognisable. Each has hold of something, and each, I think, misidentifies what it is.

Begin with what the defenders of local giving get right. There really are special obligations. A parent owes more to her own children than to children in general, and no plausible ethics of giving asks her to fund a stranger's schooling before her son's. We also owe more to those we have harmed, and to those with whom we share institutions that we sustain and from which we benefit, such as a school we attended or a cooperative to which we belong. These obligations do not arise from distance. They arise from relationships: from dependence, from history, from reciprocity.

The trouble is that the case for local giving usually trades on these relationships while asking for something else. The resident who prefers to give to a shelter in his own city rather than to a health programme abroad rarely stands in any special relation to the people in the shelter. He has not harmed them, does not depend on them and shares no institution with them beyond the accident of living within the same municipal boundary. What draws him is proximity, and proximity by itself has little moral force. A sick stranger in the next street does not matter more than a sick stranger in another country simply because she is closer, though I may be better placed to help her.

That last qualification points to the strongest argument for local giving, which is not about loyalty at all but about knowledge. Near home, donors can see whether their money is used well, and can withdraw it if it is not. This is a serious consideration, but it is an empirical one, and it cuts in both directions: where reliable assessments of distant programmes exist, the advantage of proximity shrinks, and where the local charity is opaque, it disappears. What remains, once relationships and knowledge are set aside, is often a preference for help whose results one can watch, a preference that is understandable but that should not be mistaken for an obligation.

passage: There is a familiar story about the family in South Asia. Once, it runs, people lived in large joint households: an elderly couple, their married sons with wives and children, perhaps unmarried daughters and a widowed aunt, all sharing one roof, one kitchen and one purse under the authority of the eldest man. Then came cities, salaried jobs and the ideal of the companionate couple, and the joint family began to break up into small units of parents and children. The story is told with pride by those who see the old household as a school of duty and with relief by those who see it as a school of obedience, but both versions agree about the direction of travel. It is repeated by planners, preachers and novelists alike, and it is so familiar that it is rarely asked for its evidence.

The evidence for the story is weaker than its popularity suggests. Much of it comes from counting households at a single moment, and a single moment is a poor guide to a process that unfolds over decades. A joint household is not a permanent structure but a phase. A young couple may live alone for some years; the household becomes joint when a son marries and brings his wife home; it may grow when a second son does the same; and it often divides when the father dies and the brothers set up separate hearths, each of which may in turn become joint a generation later. In a population in which every family followed this cycle exactly, a count taken on any given day would find a great many nuclear households, even though nearly everyone would spend part of life in a joint one. A high proportion of nuclear households, then, is not by itself evidence that the joint family is disappearing.

The wider theory behind the story fares little better. It was long assumed that industry produced the nuclear family, by moving work out of the home and rewarding people who could move to wherever the jobs were. Yet historians of north-western Europe found that small households of parents and children were already common there long before the factories arrived; if anything, the causation may have run partly the other way. A society's household form, it seems, is not simply read off its economy.

This is not to say that nothing has changed. Migration for work has scattered many families across cities and countries, so that brothers who would once have shared a courtyard now live hundreds of kilometres apart. But dispersal is not the same thing as dissolution. Money flows back to parents; decisions about marriages, property and the education of children are still taken together; a son abroad may be more bound by his family's expectations than a son next door. Some families keep a common fund into which brothers in different cities pay, and from which the costs of weddings and illnesses are met. A census that defines the joint family by shared residence will record such a family as several nuclear ones, and will miss the jointness that matters most to its members.

It would be equally mistaken to swing to the opposite view and declare the joint family unchanged. What is being renegotiated, often bitterly, is less the size of the household than the authority within it: whether a daughter-in-law must defer to her mother-in-law, whether elders decide whom the young marry, whether property passes to sons alone. The quarrels are often sharpest where the household is still shared, because shared space turns every question of precedence into a daily one. These are real changes, and they are better described as a transformation of jointness than as its end.

passage: National income statistics were designed to answer a question about production: how much an economy produces in a year. They were never meant to measure welfare, and some of those who built them said as much. But a statistic that is published every quarter, reported on the evening news and used to judge governments acquires a meaning beyond its design. Growth in gross domestic product has come to stand for success, and the blind spots of the measure have come to matter accordingly.

One blind spot bears directly on the environment. When a country fells a forest and sells the timber, the sale counts as production, and nothing is subtracted for the forest that is no longer there. When a country pumps oil from its fields, the revenue counts as income, though the oil in the ground was an asset and its extraction leaves the country with less of it. A household that sold a piece of its furniture every year and described the proceeds as salary would be judged to have misunderstood its own finances. National accounts already make a version of the necessary correction for machines and buildings, deducting their wear to arrive at net product; the same logic, applied consistently, would deduct the depletion of forests, fisheries, minerals and soil.

A second blind spot runs in the opposite direction. Spending that merely repairs damage counts as output. If a factory pollutes a river and the town downstream builds a treatment plant to make the water drinkable again, both the factory's production and the plant's construction add to GDP, though the town ends up with no more clean water than it had before the factory arrived. Defensive spending of this kind can make a deteriorating situation look like growth.

It does not follow that GDP should be abandoned, as some of its critics urge. For the purposes it was designed to serve, such as tracking output and employment through booms and slumps, it remains indispensable, and no alternative matches its consistency across countries and decades. Nor are the corrections straightforward. Valuing the depletion of a fishery requires assumptions about future prices and about the rate at which the stock regenerates, and different assumptions yield very different answers. The more modest and more defensible proposal is to publish, alongside GDP, accounts that record changes in natural assets, so that a country that grows by drawing down its capital can at least be seen to be doing so. A figure that is imperfect but visible is likelier to change behaviour than a correct one that nobody computes.

passage: Few words in journalism are now used with as much suspicion as objectivity. To its critics it names a pose: the pretence that reporters, alone among human beings, can step outside their own experience and describe the world from nowhere in particular. Put that way, the ideal is plainly impossible, and the critics are right to reject it. But it is worth asking whether that is the ideal anyone ever seriously defended. In at least one influential strand of its history, objectivity was proposed not as a description of the journalist but as a remedy for the journalist's limitations. Precisely because reporters could not be trusted to be neutral, the argument ran, they needed a method that would restrain what their partiality could do to the record.

The method in question resembled, in a modest way, the procedures of empirical inquiry. A claim was to be checked against more than one source; documents were to be preferred to recollection; and the reporter was to say where each piece of information came from, so that a reader or a rival could test it. On this understanding the objectivity belonged to the procedure, not to the person, much as a laboratory's results are trusted not because its scientists lack ambitions but because their work is arranged so that others can repeat it. A reporter with strong opinions could practise the method; indeed, the method existed for such reporters, since a reporter without opinions, if one could be found, would hardly need it.

What happened over the following decades was a quiet substitution. The discipline of verification, which is laborious and often invisible to the reader, was gradually overshadowed by a set of outward signs that were easier to display: a flat tone, a reluctance to draw conclusions, the habit of pairing every assertion with a counter-assertion. These signs were meant to signal fairness, but they could be produced without any verification at all. A story could quote two officials making incompatible claims, check neither, and still look objective. The appearance had detached itself from the practice it was supposed to indicate, and in some cases it obstructed that practice, since a reporter who had established that one of the officials was wrong was discouraged from saying so.

Much of the current attack on objectivity is in fact an attack on this degraded form, and to that extent it is justified. Where it goes wrong is in the alternative it sometimes proposes. If the remedy for false neutrality is for journalists to report openly from their convictions, readers are left to choose among the convictions of different reporters with no common procedure by which to test any of them. The proposal also concedes too much to the degraded form, accepting that objectivity simply is the flat tone and the paired quotation, and then discarding the whole inheritance on that basis. Candour about one's commitments is a virtue, but it is not a substitute for evidence; a frank partisan who has not checked the facts is no more reliable than a disguised one.

It should be conceded that method does not solve everything. Verification governs how a story is reported, not which stories are chosen, and the choice of what to investigate remains shaped by the interests and blind spots of those who make it. No procedure can remove that influence, and a newsroom that believes its method has made it neutral will be blind to it. Yet the concession limits the claim rather than defeating it. The case for objectivity understood as method is not that it makes journalism impartial but that it makes journalism answerable: it allows a reader who suspects a report to find out where it came from and whether it holds.

passage: The picture of the ageing mind that most people carry is one of steady decline. Memory falters, thinking slows, and the sharpness of youth gives way, from some point in early adulthood, to a long and gentle slide. The picture is not invented. On tasks that require rapid processing of unfamiliar information, such as spotting a target among distractors or holding several new items in mind while manipulating them, performance does fall with age, and the fall can be detected well before what anyone would call old age. But the picture has been assembled in a way that makes the decline look both steeper and more uniform than it is.

Much of the early evidence came from comparing people of different ages at a single moment, a method that is quick and cheap and was therefore used widely. A group of seventy-year-olds tested alongside a group of twenty-five-year-olds differs from it in more than age: the older group grew up with less schooling, different work and less familiarity with the kind of test being given. Studies that follow the same people over decades tend to show later and gentler declines than such snapshots suggest, though they carry biases of their own, since those who stay in a long study are often healthier and more able than those who drop out. Neither method gives a clean view, and the honest summary is that some decline is real, while its timing and size are less certain than the familiar picture implies.

More important, the familiar picture attends to only half of what changes. Knowledge of words, of facts, of how things usually go and how people usually behave, goes on accumulating well into later life, and on tests that draw on it older adults often outperform younger ones. Some researchers have gone further, proposing that part of the measured slowing reflects not failing machinery but a larger store: a mind that knows more words takes longer to find any one of them, much as a large library takes longer to search than a small one. The proposal is contested, and it cannot explain away every loss. It does, however, show that the same observation, a slower response, can be read as a symptom of deterioration or as a cost of accumulation, depending on what one assumes about the mind producing it.

It would be a mistake to replace the narrative of decline with an equally simple narrative of wisdom, in which age brings a serenity and judgement that compensate for everything else. Older people are not uniformly wise, and losses in speed and working memory have real consequences, for learning a new technology, for instance, or for following a fast conversation in a noisy room. The more defensible view is that ageing changes the mix of a person's capacities rather than lowering a single level, and that whether the change amounts to a loss depends on the task. In a setting that rewards speed with novel material, the young will usually have the advantage; in one that rewards the recognition of familiar patterns, a wide vocabulary or an accurate sense of how situations tend to unfold, the advantage may lie the other way. A good deal of everyday competence, from running a household to reading the mood of a tense meeting, belongs to the second kind. A society that judges older minds only by the first kind of task will find decline wherever it looks.

passage: The demonstration is by now familiar. Two groups are offered the same choice, described in two ways: a treatment that leaves ninety in a hundred patients alive after a year, or one that sees ten in a hundred die. The numbers are identical, yet the first description reliably attracts more support than the second. Since the options do not differ, the argument runs, a rational agent should not respond to the difference in wording, and the fact that people do respond is evidence that their preferences are shaped by presentation rather than substance. The principle appealed to, that logically equivalent descriptions should produce the same choice, has seemed so obvious that few have thought it needed defending.

Yet the principle is less obvious than it looks once we remember that descriptions do not fall from the sky. Somebody chooses them, and the choice is rarely arbitrary. A doctor who believes a treatment is worth trying tends, without any intent to manipulate, to speak of the patients it saves; a doctor with doubts more naturally mentions those it fails. Speakers also tend to describe a quantity in terms of the reference point from which it has moved: a glass that was full and has been partly drunk is more often called half empty than half full. If such regularities hold, then the frame carries information that the bare numbers do not, and a listener who draws an inference from it is not being swayed by mere wording. She is reading what the speaker's choice of words reveals, much as she would read an emphasis or a pause.

On this view, many framing effects are better described as sensitivity to implicit information than as failures of logic, and the experimenter who insists on equivalence has mistaken the logic of sentences for the logic of conversation. The equivalence holds between the propositions; it does not hold between the acts of uttering them, because those acts tell the hearer different things about the speaker. Participants who bring their ordinary conversational competence into the laboratory are, in a sense, being too reasonable for the experiment's purposes.

This rehabilitation should not be pushed too far. When experiments go to some lengths to make the frame visibly arbitrary, for example by assigning descriptions by an evident coin toss or by presenting both descriptions together, the inference from frame to speaker has nothing to work on, and a rational participant should set it aside. Effects in such conditions are often smaller, which is what the information account predicts, but they do not always vanish. Some residue seems to reflect the plain pull of words such as 'die' and 'lose', a reaction that would survive any amount of reflection about speakers. The information account explains a good deal of the phenomenon; it does not explain all of it.

What follows is a more discriminating verdict than either side usually offers. Whether responsiveness to a frame is a lapse depends on whether, in the situation at hand, the frame was a signal. Outside the laboratory it usually is, which is why habits formed in conversation are worth having. The danger lies precisely in that usefulness. A listener who reasonably treats frames as informative can be exploited by a speaker who knows the convention and chooses a frame to suggest a recommendation he would not dare to state outright. The fault in such cases lies less with the listener's inference than with the speaker's abuse of a norm that ordinarily makes the inference sound.

passage: Every year, research funding agencies ask panels of scientists to read hundreds of proposals and rank them, and every year the money runs out long before the list does. The proposals near the bottom are usually easy to set aside: they are poorly argued, or unoriginal, or plainly unworkable. The difficulty lies higher up. Among the proposals that every member of the panel agrees are good, the panel must still decide which will be funded and which will not, and the line it draws often separates projects that no one present could distinguish with any confidence. It is in response to this predicament that a few agencies have begun to experiment with a once unthinkable idea: setting a threshold of quality and then choosing among the proposals above it by lot.

The proposal is usually defended on grounds of efficiency. Ranking is laborious; panels spend weeks producing distinctions that a lottery would produce in minutes. This is true, but it is the weakest part of the case, and resting on it invites the reply that good decisions are worth what they cost. The stronger argument is about honesty. Experience suggests that two independent panels given the same proposals will often disagree about which of them fall just above the funding line and which just below, a sign that, near the top, the ranking reflects the composition of the panel at least as much as the merits of the work. A ranking of this kind already contains a large element of chance. What it lacks is any acknowledgement of the fact, and so its outcomes are experienced, by winners and losers alike, as verdicts on quality.

Hidden chance is not neutral chance. When the members of a panel cannot tell good proposals apart on their merits, other preferences fill the gap: a taste for methods they themselves use, a wariness of projects whose payoff is uncertain, a familiarity with applicants they have met. Each of these is a mild bias, and none need be deliberate, but together they tilt the funding line toward the safe and the recognisable. A lottery among the proposals above the threshold removes this tilt at the margin. It cannot make the panel bolder, but it can stop the panel's caution from deciding cases that its judgement cannot decide.

The most serious objection is not that lotteries abandon judgement, since judgement is exercised in full at the threshold, where panels are reasonably good at separating the sound from the unsound. It is that scientists need to believe that reward follows merit, and that a lottery, by announcing that it sometimes does not, will corrode the motivation on which research depends. This deserves to be taken seriously. Yet the belief it seeks to protect is, at the margin, already false, and a system that preserves morale by concealing how it works purchases that morale at the cost of misleading the very people it rewards. A researcher whose proposal loses a draw has at least been told the truth: that her work was judged fundable and that the money ran out.

None of this recommends lotteries everywhere. Where proposals differ in ways that can be measured, as when an agency must choose a single design for a costly instrument, ranking is the right tool and chance would be an abdication. The argument applies only where judgement has reached its limit. Its real lesson concerns not lotteries but the pretence of precision, and agencies that decline to draw lots might still learn from it, for instance by publishing how close the decisions near their funding line actually were.

passage: Complaints that the news is too gloomy are as old as newspapers themselves, and they usually take the form of an accusation: editors, it is said, prefer misery because misery sells, and they feed their readers a steady diet of disaster in the knowledge that calm and contentment do not move copies. The accusation is not exactly false, but it misplaces the problem. Most of the skew in what reaches the public does not come from a taste for bad tidings. It comes from a definition of news itself, which privileges what is sudden, unusual and attributable to a single moment. A factory that closes on a Tuesday is news; a thousand small firms that open over a decade are not, because no single day contains their story.

This definition has consequences that no individual editor intends. Events that are rare are reported precisely because they are rare, and the reporting makes them feel common. A reader who encounters three stories about aircraft accidents in a month may come away more afraid of flying than of driving, although for most travellers the ordinary hazards of the road, which seldom make headlines because they occur every day, are far greater. The same mechanism works on trends. Improvements tend to be gradual and diffuse, deteriorations are often abrupt, and so a society that is slowly getting better at something can easily believe, from its news, that it is getting worse.

It would be a mistake to answer this by demanding more good news. Stories chosen because they are cheerful would be as unrepresentative as stories chosen because they are alarming, and readers sensibly distrust outlets that seem to be managing their mood. Nor can journalism simply abandon the unusual. A fire in a crowded building matters, and the fact that most buildings do not burn is no reason to stay silent about the one that did. A press that reported only what is typical would be not more accurate but merely less useful, since the typical is, almost by definition, what its readers already expect. Novelty is a legitimate test of what deserves attention; the error lies in letting it serve as the only test.

The more promising remedy is to report the denominator alongside the numerator. A story about a crime can say whether such crimes are rising or falling; a story about a drug's side effect can say how many people take the drug without harm. A newsroom could also give slow developments a regular place, treating a ten-year change in literacy or infant survival as worthy of the front page even though nothing happened on the day it was printed. None of this asks reporters to cover less; it asks them to say more about the scale of what they cover. Such measures will not make the news a faithful miniature of the world, and they should not try to. Their aim is more modest: to ensure that what is exceptional is presented as exceptional, so that readers can tell the difference between what is striking and what is typical.

passage: Every alliance contains a quiet bargain between two fears. A state that joins an alliance worries, on the one hand, that its partner will fail it when it is attacked: this is the fear of abandonment. It worries, on the other, that its partner will drag it into a war it has no wish to fight, over interests that are not its own: this is the fear of entrapment. The two fears pull in opposite directions, and much of what passes for the routine management of alliances, the ministerial visits, the joint statements, the careful wording of guarantees, is an effort to keep them in tolerable balance.

The difficulty is that almost anything done to ease one fear aggravates the other. A state that tightens its commitment, by stationing troops on its partner's soil or promising automatic assistance, reassures the partner that it will not be abandoned. But the same assurance may embolden the partner to take risks it would otherwise avoid, confident that its ally will be obliged to follow. Loosening the commitment has the opposite effect: it restrains the partner, but it also invites the partner to doubt the alliance and perhaps to look for other friends, or to arm in ways that alarm its neighbours. There is no setting of the dial at which both fears disappear, and governments that search for one tend to lurch between them, reassuring an anxious ally one year and reining in an emboldened one the next.

For this reason, the ambiguity of many alliance commitments, often criticised as a failure of nerve, is better seen as a deliberate instrument. A guarantee that is firm enough to deter an adversary but vague about the circumstances in which it will be honoured leaves the protecting power room to judge whether its partner has provoked the crisis. The partner, uncertain whether reckless conduct will be supported, has reason to be careful; the adversary, uncertain whether aggression will be resisted, has reason to be careful too. Consider a hypothetical great power that promises to defend an island partner but declines to say whether the promise covers a dispute the partner itself might start. The silence is not an oversight. It is the policy.

The balance between the two fears is rarely the same for both members. A small state facing a powerful neighbour usually fears abandonment far more than entrapment, since it has few other places to turn, while its larger protector, with interests elsewhere and wars it would prefer not to fight, tends to fear entrapment more. Much of the friction within alliances that look harmonious from outside comes from this asymmetry: the junior partner asks for firmer pledges, the senior partner resists giving them, and each suspects the other of bad faith when each is in fact responding sensibly to its own position.

Ambiguity is not free, however. Its value depends on each party reading the uncertainty in the way the protecting power intends, and there is no guarantee that they will. An adversary may conclude that a vague commitment is a hollow one and test it, discovering too late that it was real. A partner may conclude that it will be supported whatever it does, because it cannot imagine its patron allowing it to fall. Deliberate vagueness thus trades the visible risks of a firm commitment for the hidden risk of miscalculation, which is the more dangerous for being invisible until a crisis reveals it. The strategy rewards a protecting power that understands both its partner and its adversary well, and punishes one that merely hopes it does.

passage: For much of the twentieth century, average raw scores on intelligence tests rose steadily in country after country, so steadily that the tests had to be renormed at intervals to keep the average at one hundred. The rise, which came to be called the Flynn effect after the researcher who did most to document it, presents an awkward dilemma. If the tests measure intelligence and the gains are real, then our grandparents, scored against today's norms, would have been of strikingly low intelligence, and a substantial share of them would have fallen in a range we now associate with serious intellectual difficulty. That conclusion is absurd on its face, and it is worth saying why: those generations ran farms, businesses and governments, and nobody who knew them found them obtuse. If instead the gains are an artefact of testing, it is hard to see why the artefact should be so large, so persistent and so widespread.

The way out begins with a closer look at where the gains occurred. They were not spread evenly across the tests. They were largest on tasks that ask for abstract classification and for the detection of patterns in unfamiliar material, and much smaller on tasks that draw on stored knowledge, such as vocabulary and arithmetic. Consider a person asked what a spade and a pair of shears have in common. She can answer that both are tools, or that one is used to dig the flower bed and the other to trim the hedge around it. The first answer earns credit; the second does not. Yet the second is not stupid. It reflects a habit of thinking about things in terms of their practical relations, a habit well suited to a life in which what matters about a spade is whether it will break the ground before the rain comes.

On this reading, the twentieth century did not make people more intelligent in some general sense; it trained a particular style of thought. Mass schooling, work that deals in symbols rather than objects, and a culture saturated with categories and hypotheticals rewarded the habit of setting aside what things are for and attending to what kind of thing they are. The tests, built by people who had that habit, measured it well. Nor is the spread of the habit a trivial change, since it is precisely the habit that a world of written rules, formal classifications and hypothetical planning keeps demanding of the people who live in it. The gains are therefore real, since the habit genuinely spread, but they are not gains in a single underlying power that would make the average person of today a match for the most gifted minds of a century ago.

This resolution is attractive, but it has a price that is not always acknowledged. If scores on the most abstract tests reflect habits cultivated by a particular kind of society, then the tests cannot be quite what they were often taken to be, a culture-free measure of raw capacity. They remain good predictors of success in schools and workplaces, but partly because those institutions demand the very habits the tests detect. It does not follow that the tests are worthless, or that differences in scores within a generation mean nothing; among people educated in broadly similar ways, scores can still capture real differences in how well they reason. What does follow is that comparisons across generations, and across societies with very different patterns of schooling and work, need to be interpreted with far more caution than a single number invites.
